Four Q-located intensive segments, 15 minutes each

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Community exhibition office.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Hello. Our learning group would like a small display space at the autumn event. We have been discussing several themes and need to choose one for the application.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: What is the main subject of the display you now propose?

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Water. We considered a broad energy theme, but the material we've actually prepared concerns how people interpret information about water use.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Then I'll record water as the subject.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Yes. We want to show how a comparison can be read carefully, not claim that our small classroom exercise establishes everything about household behaviour.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: A clearly defined subject will help us place the display appropriately.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Have you checked the exhibition date?

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: An early flyer mentioned the second of November.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: That was before the venue booking was confirmed. The event is now on the fifth of November.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: The fifth is possible for our group. I'll replace the flyer in our shared folder so nobody organises transport for the old date.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Thank you. The confirmation will include the revised date and the setup instructions.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We'll work from that version. We've learned that saying a date changed isn't enough if the old file remains the easiest one for volunteers to find when they're making their own arrangements.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: What time can we bring in the display?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Your allocated setup slot begins at two twenty-five in the afternoon. The public event opens later, but we bring groups in at different times to keep the entrance usable.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Two twenty-five, then. I had assumed two o'clock because that's when setup begins generally.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Two is the first group's time, not yours. Please use the allocated slot unless we confirm a change.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: I'll put the exact time on our transport plan and ask the volunteers to arrive together.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: That will help the team match each group with its space without several separate arrivals searching for the same booking.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: How many tables will you need?

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We first imagined using three, but we've simplified the display. Two tables should be enough.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: I'll enter two on the booking. Please send the outline showing how you intend to use them.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We can place the comparison activity on one and the explanation on the other.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Good. The outline helps us check the available space; it isn't a request for a fully finished visual design today.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: That's useful. We'd rather confirm the practical arrangement before printing everything, and we don't want to reserve a third table that would remain mostly empty during the event.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: What is the total space fee?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: For your community group, the confirmed fee is sixty pounds.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Does that include both tables?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Yes, sixty pounds is the total for the agreed space and those two tables. Additional services, if requested, would be discussed separately.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: I'll record the total rather than multiplying it by the number of tables.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Exactly. The confirmation will list the arrangement so you can check that it matches our discussion.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Our volunteer handling the budget will appreciate that. A single unexplained amount on a message can be difficult to interpret when people weren't part of the original booking conversation.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: What should we bring apart from the display itself?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Please prepare labels for any loose pieces used in the activity. Similar pieces from neighbouring displays can become mixed up during packing.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Labels, then. We'll put our group code on them and keep a matching list.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: That's helpful. You don't need to attach labels to the venue's furniture; the tables already have their own identifiers.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: I'll make the distinction clear. We'll label our activity pieces, not everything in the space.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Good. The aim is to help return each object to the right group, rather than cover the venue's existing instructions with new information.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Does the display need a professional presenter? Our volunteers know the activity well but aren't used to speaking to large audiences.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: No. Your space is designed for short conversations with small groups. Prepare a clear introduction and let visitors ask questions.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: So we don't need a stage performance?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: That's right. A short practice with somebody unfamiliar with the activity may be more useful than learning a long speech.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We can do that at our next meeting. It should reveal which words need explanation before visitors encounter the comparison, rather than relying on the volunteers to improvise a different introduction every time.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: Can we collect visitors' contact details for future events?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Only through a separate, clearly explained sign-up arrangement that visitors can choose to use. Participation in your activity should not require joining your mailing list.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We'll keep the activity response sheet separate from an optional sign-up sheet.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Good. Make the purpose of each clear, and follow the event's contributor arrangements.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We don't need contact details to understand how someone interpreted the display, so there is no reason to put them on that response sheet.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Exactly. Keeping different purposes distinct helps visitors understand what they are agreeing to and helps your team manage the resulting records appropriately.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: If a visitor asks whether the display proves that one household is more responsible than another, how should we respond?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Explain the limits of the comparison you've prepared. The activity is intended to help people examine information, and the figures may not support that personal judgement.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We can show the assumptions and describe what additional information would be needed.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: That sounds appropriate. Don't turn a convenient illustration into a claim that goes beyond its evidence simply because a visitor wants a simple ranking.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: We'll practise that explanation as well as the introduction. It is part of helping people understand the display, not an awkward question to avoid.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: How will the final display location be confirmed?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: We'll send a numbered plan with your booking reference. Please use that plan rather than the early layout on the event notice.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: And if it changes?

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: We will send a direct revision identifying your new location. Don't arrange an informal exchange with another group without contacting the team, because the plan also supports setup and access arrangements.

turns.speaker: Exhibitor
turns.text: I'll make one current copy available to all our volunteers.

turns.speaker: Officer
turns.text: Excellent. That reduces the chance that different members arrive with different plans and each assumes the other person has misunderstood where the group belongs.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: Welcome to the exhibition learning area. North is at the top of your diagram, and the entrance is on the southern edge. The central garden is our reference point. The lettered spaces around it are separate activity areas, not a sequence of numbered stops. Check-in is directly south of the garden, on the entrance axis. It isn't in either southern corner. Exhibitors should report there before moving equipment into a display space. The team will confirm your location and tell you whether setup is ready. A printed plan is useful, but the check-in team may have a confirmed update that was issued after your copy was downloaded.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: The demonstration area is in the north-west corner. The first draft placed demonstrations directly north of the garden, but that space now has another purpose. On the current map, the demonstration area lies west of the northern central space and diagonally north-west of the garden. Demonstrations are short scheduled activities, so an apparently quiet moment may be the changeover between presenters. Please ask the coordinator before placing equipment there. The timetable helps several groups share the area without assuming that one group's arrival gives it priority over another. For your map answer, use the north-west letter rather than the letter directly above the garden.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: The quiet discussion area is directly east of the garden, level with its centre on the diagram. It isn't the room in the south-east corner. We use it for conversations that need more time than the brief exchanges beside a busy display. That doesn't mean it is reserved for every exhibitor throughout the event. Check the arrangement with the team before inviting a group to move there. If the area is occupied, staff can explain the available options. Please avoid promising a private conversation in a space merely because you saw empty chairs earlier. The current use may have changed by the time your visitors arrive.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: The feedback station is in the north-east corner, directly north of the quiet discussion area. It is east of the northern central space, since those two positions lie on the same row. We have kept feedback separate from check-in so visitors can leave comments after exploring the displays without mixing with arriving exhibitors. The station collects the event's general feedback. It doesn't automatically collect responses for every individual group's project. If you are using your own activity sheet, explain where visitors should return it. Clear collection arrangements prevent useful comments from ending up in a pile whose purpose nobody can later identify.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: At the end of the event, groups collect stored packaging from the collection area in the south-west corner. That is west of check-in and on the opposite side of the map from the south-east space. Please use your group code when asking for the packaging. Similar boxes can be difficult to distinguish by appearance alone, especially after a busy day. The collection team will explain the order for moving items back towards the entrance. Do not assume that collecting a box means your vehicle can immediately enter the setup route. The closing arrangement depends on the whole site, including visitors who may still be leaving other activities.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: Each display should distinguish a question from a conclusion. A heading that asks why two figures differ invites investigation; a heading that announces one explanation has already made a stronger claim. Visitors may remember the heading more readily than a qualification in small print. The exhibition team therefore asks groups to review their main wording as carefully as their detailed notes. This doesn't require making every display uncertain about everything. It requires matching the strength of the claim to the evidence actually presented. A clear limited conclusion can be more informative than an impressive broad statement that the activity cannot support when somebody asks how it was reached.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: When a visitor gives an unexpected answer, ask how they reached it before assuming they misunderstood. They may have noticed a feature your team overlooked, interpreted a label differently or used information from elsewhere. A short neutral follow-up can reveal which of those possibilities is relevant. Avoid immediately correcting the visitor in a way that hides the reasoning you wanted to understand. If the activity has a factual explanation, you can still provide it after hearing their account. The point is to distinguish understanding a person's reasoning from simply checking whether their final answer matches the one printed in your facilitator notes.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: If you revise an explanation during the event, record the change and when it was introduced. A clearer phrase may improve the visitor experience, but it also means responses before and after the change were produced under different conditions. Combining them without a note can make a small evaluation difficult to interpret. The revision log doesn't need to become a long diary of every conversation. It should identify the wording or procedure changed, the reason and the point in the session when the new version began. That is enough to help your later review connect an apparent change in responses with a possible change in the activity itself.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: A technical problem should be reported to the event support team using the location and equipment identifier. Saying that the screen near the plants isn't working may describe more than one item. A clear identifier helps the team find the problem without leaving other groups searching for someone who has gone to the wrong area. If the interactive element is unavailable, use the alternative activity prepared in your plan and explain the change to visitors. Don't present responses from the alternative as though they came from the original version. Both may be useful, but the distinction matters when your group later discusses what the activity achieved.

turns.speaker: Exhibition host
turns.text: Before packing, complete the brief stage review with your group. Identify what you intended visitors to do, what you observed and what remains uncertain. Include one feature to retain and one change to test next time. The review isn't a demand to prove that every part of the display succeeded. It is a way to turn the event into useful evidence for the next decision. If your conclusions depend mainly on enthusiastic comments from a few visitors, say so. Those comments can be valuable without representing everybody who passed the space. A clear account of the limits helps the next version address the right problem.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your display pilot begins tomorrow. Do you both support testing it with people outside your course?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Yes. Our classmates already know the terminology and may overlook an unclear label.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: I initially thought recruiting outside the course would take too long. We have four volunteers available now, so I support it.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What can four volunteers tell you?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: They can reveal specific difficulties, though we shouldn't call their responses representative of all exhibition visitors.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Exactly. We'll ask them to explain what they think the activity is asking before giving the full explanation. That should make a hidden assumption visible while there is still time to revise the wording.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Owen suggests putting the entire introduction on one screen.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: I favour that. Visitors would see the purpose before beginning, instead of moving through several short pages.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: I'd keep the introduction in two stages. One screen could contain too much information for somebody standing beside a busy display.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Could shorter wording make one screen workable?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Perhaps, but I still prefer separating the task from the background explanation.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: I continue to support one screen, with only the essential information.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then you disagree about the presentation structure, not whether visitors need an introduction. Record that distinction so your next test compares a clear proposal rather than two vaguely different designs.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Do you want to keep written observer notes as well as the interaction log?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Yes. The log records selections, but it won't show that someone reread a label or asked what a term meant.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: I would leave the notes out of this first test. We have limited staff, and taking detailed notes could distract the facilitator from running the activity consistently.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: We can use a short structured sheet, but I still support keeping notes.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Owen, does a shorter sheet change your position?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: Not for tomorrow's pilot. I'd prioritise a stable procedure and discuss observations immediately afterwards.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Then my preference remains, but we haven't agreed to implement it.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Your draft proposes ranking visitors by how quickly they finish. Why?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: I thought a ranking might make the activity entertaining.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: I don't support it. Speed isn't the understanding we're trying to investigate, and a public ranking might make people rush.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: On reflection, I agree. I'll remove the ranking from the design.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you also abandoning all timing information?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: That's a separate question. I am withdrawing the public ranking, not deciding every possible use of timing.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Good distinction. We can discuss a private measure of task duration without turning it into a competition.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then neither of you supports the ranking at the end of this discussion.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Should you record how long the first attempt takes?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: I support recording first-attempt completion time. It may identify a stage where the procedure takes longer than we planned.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: I wouldn't add timing in this pilot. I'd rather ask participants to explain the comparison and see whether the language is clear.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: We could record time without displaying it to visitors. I still favour it as a practical measure, not a score of ability.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Amira?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: I understand that narrower purpose, but I still prefer to leave it out tomorrow.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: So Owen supports the timing proposal, while Amira remains against adding it to this particular pilot.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What about recording revisions made between pilot sessions?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: We need a revision log. Otherwise we may forget which participants saw which wording.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: Agreed. I first imagined overwriting the display file after each change, but then the earlier version would be difficult to reconstruct.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: We'll give each version a label and record the reason for a change.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Does that require a lengthy report every time?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: No. A short entry can identify what changed, when and why.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Then we both support the log as part of the procedure. It should preserve the link between feedback and revision, rather than become a list of changes detached from the problem each one addressed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two content changes have you agreed after the first pilot?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Explain how the comparison was made. Several visitors assumed the two figures described identical circumstances, but that wasn't stated.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: Yes. We'll add a brief explanation of what was held the same and what differed.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Are you adding an animation to make the numbers more dramatic?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: No, that wouldn't resolve the misunderstanding we observed.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Nor are we adding another organisation's logo to imply support.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then your first agreed change is methodological: tell visitors what the comparison actually compares, so they can assess the claim rather than fill an information gap with an assumption.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: And the second agreed content change?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: Make missing values visible instead of leaving an unexplained blank.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Agreed. One visitor treated a blank as zero, while another thought the display had failed to load.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Will you fill the blank with a typical value to simplify the task?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: No. That would turn missing information into an observation we never collected.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: We also rejected a headline claiming that the display proves the cause of the difference.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Good. The two revisions are an explanation of the comparison and an explicit indication of missing values. They help visitors interpret the available evidence without manufacturing a stronger result than the material supports.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Which two limitations should appear in your pilot report?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: First, the activity was tested in only one venue. We don't know whether the same instructions would work equally well in a noisier or more crowded setting.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: Agreed. We can describe the setting we used, but we shouldn't write as though we've tested every exhibition context.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Is saving the files in a shared folder a limitation?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: No, that helped us keep the records available.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: And the display did run, so a total technical failure isn't part of this pilot's history.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Exactly. State the conditions that actually limit the claim, not a list of difficulties a project might have experienced.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What is the second limitation?

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: The facilitator gave different amounts of help to different participants. A few completed the activity after receiving an extra explanation that others didn't hear.

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Yes. Their completion can't be attributed only to the display wording.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: What will you change?

turns.speaker: Amira
turns.text: Prepare a consistent assistance procedure and record when extra help is given.

turns.speaker: Owen
turns.text: We don't need to pretend the earlier sessions never happened; we need to explain why the results require caution.

turns.speaker: Tutor
turns.text: Then the two limitations are one venue and inconsistent assistance. Using the same colour scheme throughout isn't an additional limitation by itself, provided the information remained readable.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: This lecture follows a fictional team preparing an evidence review for a community project. Its first stage defines the question. A broad interest in whether information helps people make decisions must become a question precise enough to guide the review. The team specifies the setting, the kind of information and the outcome it wants to examine. Those choices do not guarantee a simple answer, but they make the boundaries visible. Without them, the team may collect attractive examples that address different problems and then treat their variety as if it were a clear body of evidence for one claim. The question determines what a useful answer would need to explain.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The second stage maintains a search log. The log records where the team looked, the terms it used and the limits it applied. This makes the search process traceable rather than relying on somebody's memory of finding an interesting document. It also helps identify gaps that a later stage might address. A search log does not prove that every relevant item has been found. It describes the process actually used, including practical constraints. The team should distinguish a planned search from a completed one, so readers don't assume that a source was checked merely because its name appeared in an early proposal or on a list of possible places to investigate.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The third stage uses an extraction sheet to record comparable details from each included source. The sheet might capture the setting, participants, method, outcome and stated limitations. The team tests the sheet on a small sample before using it throughout the review. If different readers interpret a field differently, the wording or guidance needs attention. The aim is not to force every source into identical categories when important differences exist. It is to preserve enough consistent information to support a reasoned comparison while keeping relevant differences visible. A short quotation or page reference can help another reader check how a particular entry was derived from the original source.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fourth stage conducts an appraisal of the evidence. Appraisal means examining how well a source's method supports the claim being considered. An impressive title, a polished graph or a confident conclusion is not a substitute for that examination. A source may be useful for describing an experience but weak for establishing why an outcome occurred. Another may address a narrow causal question in a setting unlike the community project. The team should record both strengths and limits rather than attach a single unexplained quality label. Appraisal connects the review question with the evidence available and helps prevent a relevant-looking source from being asked to support a claim beyond its method.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The fifth stage produces a synthesis. The synthesis brings the evidence together through an explanation of patterns, differences and uncertainty. It is not simply a sequence of short summaries with a confident final sentence attached. The team needs to show which sources address sufficiently similar questions to be compared and where differences make a combined statement difficult. If findings conflict, the review should investigate possible reasons rather than count positive and negative conclusions as though every source had equal relevance and strength. A useful synthesis lets readers trace the final interpretation back to the sources and understand why some findings carry more weight for the specific question than others.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Publication bias is one possible limitation of an evidence collection. Studies with striking or favourable results may be easier to find than work whose results attracted less attention. A review based only on prominent examples could therefore give a distorted impression of the whole body of work. The team should consider its search process and explain what kinds of material it was able to locate. This doesn't justify assuming that every missing study would contradict the visible evidence. It identifies a reason for caution about treating the available collection as complete. Acknowledging the possibility helps readers understand the difference between the evidence located and every investigation that may have been carried out.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Heterogeneity means differences among the included studies that matter to interpretation. The studies may involve different participants, settings, procedures or definitions of the outcome. Some differences may be small enough for a particular comparison, while others change what the results mean. The team should describe the important differences rather than assume that a shared keyword makes the studies interchangeable. A combined numerical result can look precise while hiding incompatible measurements. In other cases, examining variation can reveal useful questions about when an approach works and under what conditions. The review should therefore treat heterogeneity as something to understand, not merely an inconvenience to remove from a cleaner-looking presentation.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: The strength of a recommendation should reflect confidence in the relevant evidence. Confidence depends on more than how many sources point in the same direction. Their methods, relevance, consistency and missing information all matter. The team may have enough evidence to suggest a small reversible trial while remaining uncertain about a large permanent change. That is a reasoned difference in the scale of a recommendation, not a contradiction. The report should explain what it is confident about and what remains open. A reader can then judge whether the proposed next step is proportionate to the evidence, rather than treating a recommendation as proof that every uncertainty has been settled.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: Transferability concerns whether evidence from one setting can inform another. A method tested with experienced participants in a quiet room may work differently for first-time visitors at a crowded event. The review should compare the conditions that are relevant to the proposed use and identify which differences could matter. It should not assume that every difference makes the evidence useless, or that an appealing result applies everywhere without adjustment. A small local trial may help examine the most important uncertainty. The purpose is to connect existing knowledge to a new decision carefully, while keeping the reasoning visible enough for others to challenge or improve it.

turns.speaker: Lecturer
turns.text: At the final stage review, the team creates a decision record. This record identifies the proposed next action, the evidence supporting it, the main uncertainties and the conditions that would lead the team to reconsider. It also distinguishes actions already approved from suggestions that still need discussion. The record is not a promise that the project will never change direction. It provides a basis for explaining a later change when new information arrives. In that way, a review becomes part of an ongoing learning process: the next trial has a purpose, its results can be compared with expectations, and the team can explain how evidence influenced what it chose to do.
